Galatians
guh-LAY-shunz
noun (proper)
From Greek Galatai (Γαλάται) — the Galatians, inhabitants of the Roman province of Galatia in central Asia Minor; the title of Paul's most polemical letter, written in direct combat against the Judaizing assault on justification by faith alone, which Luther called his “Katherine von Bora.”

Biblical Definition

The Epistle to the Galatians is Paul's most urgent and combative letter — widely dated either to AD 48–49 (South Galatia theory) or the mid-50s (North Galatia theory). It responds to Judaizing teachers who had infiltrated the Galatian congregations and insisted that circumcision and Law-observance were required for justification alongside faith. Paul opens without his customary thanksgiving and moves immediately to a double anathema against any gospel-alteration: “let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8). The doctrinal heart is chapters 2–3: justification is by faith in Christ alone, not by works of the Law. “Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.” (Gal 2:16). Abraham believed God and was counted righteous before circumcision was given (Gal 3:6–9), proving that faith-righteousness preceded and supersedes ceremonial Law. Christ redeemed His people from the Law's curse by becoming a curse in their place: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law — having become a curse for us” (Gal 3:13). The freedom Christ purchased is not license but liberation from the enslaving demand for self-achieved righteousness: “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.” (Gal 5:1). Martin Luther's Commentary on Galatians (1535) shaped the entire Reformation's theological vocabulary. The 1689 LBCF's article on justification (ch. 11) flows directly from Galatians' categories.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster does not record “Galatians” as a common English noun; it names the recipients of Paul's canonical letter — the New Testament's definitive exposition of justification by faith alone and the apostolic death sentence over any supplementation of the gospel.

GALATIANS, n. pl. [From Galatia, a province of central Asia Minor settled by Celtic peoples in the third century BC.] The inhabitants of the Roman province of Galatia; specifically, the recipients of the Apostle Paul's most polemical epistle — a letter defending justification by faith alone against the Judaizing heresy that sought to add circumcision and Law-observance to the ground of acceptance before God.

The Reformers recognized Galatians as the charter document of evangelical freedom — the apostolic proof that any addition to the finished work of Christ for justification is not a stricter gospel but a false gospel under apostolic anathema.

Luther's Commentary on Galatians (1535), Calvin's commentary, and John Owen's exposition form a unified Reformed reading: “works of the Law” encompasses every human moral effort to secure divine acceptance, not merely ethnic Jewish markers — and the double anathema stands over every supplementation, ancient or modern.

Key Scripture

Gal 1:8 — "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed."

Gal 2:16 — "Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified."

Gal 3:13 — "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:"

Gal 5:1 — "Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage."

Modern Corruption

Rome never conceded Galatians; the “New Perspective on Paul” school redefines “works of the Law” as ethnic boundary markers rather than instruments of self-righteousness, gutting the letter's Reformation application.

expand to see more

The Judaizing error Galatians combats has never been extinguished; it has only changed forms. The Roman Catholic Council of Trent (1547) condemned justification by faith alone, insisting that infused righteousness and sacramental cooperation contribute to the basis of acceptance before God. The “New Perspective on Paul” scholars (E. P. Sanders, James D. G. Dunn, N. T. Wright) recast Paul's “works of the Law” as sociological boundary markers (food laws, circumcision, Sabbath) rather than as humanity's general attempt to merit divine favor — narrowing the letter's scope and softening its assault on all works-righteousness. This reframing has found welcome hearing in progressive evangelical circles precisely because it allows retention of Pauline language while removing the Reformation's nerve.

The Reformed confessional tradition holds the Reformation reading: “works of the Law” encompasses every human moral effort to secure divine acceptance, not merely ethnic Jewish praxis. Luther's reading was not anachronistic; it was apostolic. Galatians' double anathema (1:8–9) targets any supplementation of Christ's atoning obedience as the exclusive ground of justification — including Rome's infused righteousness, the prosperity gospel's activating faith, and progressive theology's justice-works as signals of authentic discipleship.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Rooted in the name of the Celtic-descended peoples who settled central Asia Minor and the Greek pistis (“faith”) — the letter's ruling theological category over against every form of works-righteousness.

expand to see more

Galatia — a Roman province of central Asia Minor, home to Celtic (Galatian) settlers from the third century BC; Paul founded churches there on his first and second missionary journeys (Acts 13–14, 16:6)

Greek pistis (πίστις) — faith, trust, confidence; the singular instrument of justification throughout the letter as opposed to erga nomou (works of the Law)

Greek dikaiosynē (δικαιοσύνη) — righteousness; in Galatians always the God-given status declared over the believer, never the merit of legal performance

Greek anathema (ἀνάθεμα) — accursed, devoted to destruction; Paul's severity in Gal 1:8–9 signals that gospel-alteration is not a secondary dispute but a first-order defection from the apostolic word

Latin sola fide — faith alone; the Reformation's crystallization of Galatians' central argument, denied by Rome and the Judaizers alike, recovered at Wittenberg and Geneva as the article on which the church stands or falls

Usage

"Galatians' double anathema (1:8–9) is the biblical warrant for the Reformed principle that doctrinal boundaries on justification are not optional: any teaching that places works alongside faith as a ground of acceptance is not a stricter form of Christianity but its negation."

"Martin Luther's Commentary on Galatians (1535) shaped the Reformation's vocabulary; Calvin's commentary and Owen's exposition follow its Pauline grammar — a unified confessional stream confirming that the Galatian letter's meaning was not invented in the sixteenth century but recovered from apostolic ground."

"The pastoral application of Galatians is not merely historical: every time a church conditions acceptance on political alignment, ethnic solidarity, or therapeutic performance, the Galatian heresy has returned in contemporary dress and the anathema stands."
